edbDesc: The formation of vapour bubbles in a flowing liquid in a region where the pressure of the liquid falls below its vapour pressure. Usually divided into two classes of behavior. Inertial (or transient) cavitation occurs when a void or bubble in a liquid rapidly collapses, producing a shock wave. Non-inertial cavitation is the process in which a bubble in a fluid is forced to oscillate in size or shape due to energy input, e.g. acoustic field.
title: Cavitation
description: Where a liquid moves fast or is shaken hard, its pressure drops so low that vapour bubbles appear, then collapse violently. Charles Parsons found in 1894 that this was what stopped his turbine ship Turbinia's propellers from gripping the water, and why they pitted. The same collapsing bubbles scrub jewellery clean in ultrasonic baths.
effect: low pressure in a fast or shaken liquid makes bubbles that collapse violently
strength: Each collapsing bubble briefly reaches thousands of atmospheres, enough to pit a bronze propeller over weeks.
pickWhy: A specific effect that does real work (cleaning, mixing, breaking things up); Acoustic Cavitation here and Hydrodynamic Cavitation and Supercavitation in other batches merge into it. Dated to Parsons's propeller trials on Turbinia, when it was first recognised and named.
